title: Sell Mineral Rights in Otsego County, MI
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Otsego County, MI
metaDescription: Otsego County, MI mineral owner? Gaylord-area Antrim Shale interests, honest talk on decline and pricing, no mailbox-offer games. Get a real evaluation.
heroLead: Otsego County sat dead center of the Antrim Shale drilling boom, and thirty years later that means most owners here are dealing with a mature stripper-well interest, not the gusher their granddad's lease papers made it sound like.
intro: Gaylord is the county seat of Otsego County and the hub for pretty much everything oil and gas in this part of the state, from the old field offices to the equipment yards you still see off I-75. Otsego County was one of the most heavily drilled Antrim Shale counties in Michigan during the boom years, which is good news and bad news for a mineral owner today. Good news because there's a well-documented production history to check your interest against. Bad news because most of those wells are now decades into a long, flat decline and the checks reflect it.

We evaluate mineral and royalty interests all over Otsego County, from the ground right around Gaylord out to Vanderbilt and Johannesburg and the farm sections in between. A lot of what we see is heirship property, land that's been in a family since the homestead era with the minerals split off from the surface somewhere along the way, and the current owner has no real idea what the interest is worth or even exactly what they hold.

sections.heading: The Antrim boom hit Otsego County harder than most
paragraphs: During the peak years of Section 29 tax-credit drilling, roughly 1986 through 1998, Otsego County saw a dense pattern of Antrim Shale wells go in on tight spacing, often 40 or 80-acre units. That density means if your family owned land anywhere in the county during that period, there's a decent chance a well got drilled on or near it, and a lease got signed that's still technically in effect today held by production.

The operators active here have changed hands repeatedly. Ward Lake Energy and Miller Exploration were common names in the original leases, and a lot of that production has since consolidated under larger holding entities. If the company name on your royalty statement doesn't match what's on your original lease, that's just the industry's normal churn, not a sign anything's wrong.

sections.heading: What a mature Antrim well actually pays now
paragraphs: Antrim Shale gas is biogenic, produced by bacteria in the shale rather than heat and pressure, and it sits shallow. That geology gives these wells a long, flat decline curve rather than the steep drop-off you'd see in a deep conventional gas well. But flat doesn't mean strong. Thirty-plus years in, most Otsego County Antrim wells are producing a small fraction of their peak-year volumes, and royalty checks that ran real money a month in the 1990s are now often down to a trickle.

We're not going to tell you your interest is worth what it was worth in 1995, because it isn't, and any buyer quoting you a number based on old peak production is either not looking at your actual statements or hoping you won't ask questions.

sections.heading: Split estate and heirship in Otsego County
paragraphs: A lot of the mineral ownership in this county is split from the surface, meaning the person farming the land or living on it doesn't own what's underneath it. That happens when an earlier owner sold the surface but kept the minerals, or vice versa, sometimes generations back. If you're getting a small royalty check but don't own or live on the surface property tied to it, that's a normal split-estate setup, not a mistake.

Heirship is the other common wrinkle. Otsego County's register of deeds in Gaylord holds the recorded chain of title, and if a mineral interest passed down through a will or intestate succession without ever being formally divided among heirs, you may be one of several cousins each holding a fractional share of a fractional share. Sorting that out is usually the first real step before any sale.

sections.heading: How we look at value on an Otsego County interest
paragraphs: We start with your actual royalty statements or division order, not a guess, and check them against recent production and current operator activity in your specific section, township, and range. Net mineral acres, well economics, remaining reserve life, and whether there's realistic potential for an offset well or workover nearby all factor into where we land. On a mature Antrim interest, that often means the honest answer is a modest lump sum reflecting a modest remaining income stream, and we'll tell you that straight rather than dress it up.

If your interest looks like it's worth more held than sold, meaning the steady small checks over time beat a lump sum, we'll say so. We'd rather give you the real math than a number designed to get a signature.

faqs.question: Why did drilling activity in Otsego County slow down so much after the 1990s?
faqs.answer: The Section 29 federal tax credit that made a lot of Antrim Shale drilling economical expired at the end of 2002, and by then most of the easily accessible core acreage in the county had already been drilled. What's left today is mostly legacy production from those original wells, still running but well past peak.

faqs.question: How do I find out what mineral interest I actually own in Otsego County?
faqs.answer: Start at the Otsego County register of deeds office in Gaylord and pull the deed or probate record showing the transfer to you. If an operator has ever paid you, ask for a copy of your division order, which spells out your decimal interest in the well.

faqs.question: Is a lump-sum sale better than keeping my small monthly royalty check?
faqs.answer: It depends on your situation. A lump sum trades a stream of small, uncertain future checks for one payment now. Some owners want that, others would rather keep collecting even a modest check indefinitely. We'll run the numbers on your specific interest and give you both sides before you decide.

faqs.question: Somebody offered me a flat per-acre price without asking about my well. Is that normal?
faqs.answer: It's common, but it's a red flag on accuracy. A responsible offer accounts for your specific well's production history and remaining life, not a blanket county-wide number. Get your actual statements looked at before accepting anything like that.

faqs.question: What documents should I have ready before contacting a mineral buyer in Otsego County?
faqs.answer: Your deed or probate document showing ownership, your most recent royalty statement or division order, and if you have it, the legal description with section, township, and range. That's usually enough for a first real look at your interest.
